en: The *Mañjuśrī-mahā-samaya-sūtra*, spoken by the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, contains the *Dharmacakra of the Command for the Elimination of Calamities*,
specifically the chapter on "Pacifying Calamities and Removing Difficulties," also known as the *Chesting* (Blazing).
The Light of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva arose from the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Surveying the great assembly, he spoke these words:
"I observe that all sentient beings,
since beginningless time, have wandered through the cycle of birth and death."
Enshrouded by deluded karma, they harbor mutual love and hatred;
they experience various karmic retributions and invite manifold calamities.
I, relying upon the sustaining power and spiritual authority of all Tathāgatas, [act as follows].
Briefly stated, this concerns the provisional means that accord with the world:
the teaching for eliminating calamities and obstacles,
and the *śāntika* maṇḍala ritual for commanding the devas.
The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, speaks thus in accordance with the realm of sentient beings:
"In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I heard this sublime Dharma from the presence of the Buddha Śālarāja."
I shall now explain it;
you should listen well.
This Dharma is profound and subtle, its intended meaning difficult to comprehend; one should seek instruction and receive its study from a Mahā-ācārya of the transmitted teachings.
Furthermore, one must carefully select an auspicious time and day according to the *nakṣatras* and *tithis*,
personally receive the mantras, mudrās, and homa rituals,
and install the painted image and the wheel of the *ājñā*.
A monk who receives this instruction must ensure that his physical and mental precepts are pure.
He must not violate the four grave prohibitions or the ten major precepts.
If he has committed such violations, he should not perform this recitation for others.
On the contrary, it will instead invite calamity and fail to produce any efficacy.
A person who upholds the Dharma must always maintain purity.
If one acts on behalf of a king, one should construct a maṇḍala.
Some knead five-colored powders;
others use pigments to paint the distinct forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and devas,
arranging their internal and external positions according to their respective ranks and order of honor.
One must perform this with careful composure and secrecy.
With a profound heart of reverence and a resolute aspiration, one will surely obtain its efficacious response;
calamities shall be extinguished and merit and virtue shall grow.
Like an echo responding to a sound, there is no request that will not be fulfilled.
Do not allow those who do not believe in cause and effect, the heterodox followers of wrong views,
or the ignorant, shallow-minded, and deluded people to [obstruct this].
Furthermore, when butchers, executioners, the five types of caṇḍālas,
eunuchs, slaves, prostitutes, and others of such kind catch sight of this wheel,
they immediately give rise to slander.
Both the maker and the slanderer suffer loss.
The forms of the devas are not meant for ordinary, ignorant people to see at will;
if they are treated with contempt or displayed publicly, the spirits will be displeased.
Thus, blessings and protection are difficult to invoke;
if one does not maintain secrecy, the practitioner will incur blame, and all ritual arrangements will be in vain.
Such people of shallow intelligence fail to comprehend the Tathāgata’s skillful means of great compassion and the majestic power of mantras.
By means of his skillful wisdom, the Buddha’s instructions, and his transformative empowerment,
he caused the sun, moon, stars, and the hosts of celestial beings roaming through space to give rise to hearts of compassion.
The Tathāgata has already proclaimed this in such sūtras as the Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta, the Sūryagarbha, and the Candragarbha;
it has also been frequently manifested in other assemblies.
I shall now explain it clearly for you.
The Ritual for the Maṇḍala of Peaceful Recitation, detailing the sequence for the arrangement of the altar.
If there should be eclipses of the sun or moon within a kingdom’s borders,
or if the five planets lose their proper course and undergo changes in form and color;
Or when malevolent stars, comets, or meteors oppress the natal constellations (*nakṣatra*) of kings or persons of noble rank;
or when the sun and moon suffer eclipses within the palace of one’s own birth-sign—
at such times, one should employ this teaching for the *śānti-homa* (propitiatory fire ritual).
Should a great pestilence arise, diseases spread, or spirits and ghosts cause violent disturbances;
or should soldiers and bandits from foreign lands invade and plunder the people of the country—
if there be a wise person who perceives these events beforehand:
One should petition for the establishment of the maṇḍala.
The sovereign should, day by day, give rise to a mind of profound devotion and personally make vows to pray for the bestowal of protective empowerment.
One will certainly attain victory and evil thieves shall be extinguished.

If there are people in the world who suddenly encounter calamities, such as difficulties with kings or difficulties with bandits, or are entangled in legal disputes with government officials, or are oppressed by enemies; [they shall be saved].
Afflicted by a malignant illness that persists despite medical treatment,
at such a time, one fears imminent peril and disaster.
If there are karmic debts from past lives, or if one faces life-threatening calamities and fatal perils,
one should immediately rely on this teaching to create and establish the Maṇḍala of the Dharma-Wheel for the Elimination of Calamities according to the ritual procedures.
Performing recitation with secret diligence and empowerment,
pray with sincere devotion to the assembly of holy deities and celestial lords:
"May all calamities be dispelled, and may I obtain every auspiciousness."
One should sprinkle and sweep a single clean room.
Taking gomasī (cow dung) that has not yet reached the ground with a white ox-hide,
one should mix it with white sandalwood scented water and auspicious incense, and smear it all over the floor.
Furthermore, one should repeatedly sprinkle scented water upon the house and its four walls to make them utterly pure;
therein, one should draw this wheel for pacifying calamities.
If one constructs a maṇḍala ground altar,
one must dig the earth according to the instructions,
removing all impure substances, broken tiles, and shattered vessels.
Skulls, hair, chaff, husks, ashes, charcoal;
dung beetles and various other insects and venomous stinging creatures;
as well as thorns, bones, rotten wood, gravel, stones, sand, and grit.
Separately take firm, high-quality white earth from a riverbank that has a sweet taste;
mix it with incense and pack it down until it is extremely solid.
Then, smear and polish it according to the ritual rules.
First, have the painters abstain from alcohol, meat, and the five pungent roots, and remain far removed from sensual desire.
They shall bathe with fragrant water, put on fresh and clean garments, and at the break of dawn,
receive the eight precepts of the *aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*.
Upon a clean white hide or a clean white cloth,
draw this twelve-spoked golden wheel;
if one is constructing an earth maṇḍala, [it should be drawn there].
One should then knead five-colored powders;
each individual color of powder should be consecrated separately with the mantra seven times.
Or recite it twenty-one times before using it. Or else,
one may depict it with colored pigments.
For three days and three nights, or seven days and seven nights,
once the rites for seeking blessings are completed, one must immediately withdraw [the ritual implements].
If it is an altar of the earth, one should remove the physical images.
One should not remain for long,
lest insects and rats defile or trample it,
or that people of inferior intellect, those with false views, or non-Buddhist outsiders might see it.
If those such as the five types of caṇḍālas, eunuchs, slaves, and so forth should see it,
all the noble ones will be displeased and, conversely, one will incur blame.
This is especially true if one intends to take it on a long journey.
One should then paint it in colors upon white leather or silk cloth,
measuring either one cubit or two cubits square;
at most, it shall not exceed three or four cubits.
According to his own capacity, he delineated the forms of more than seventy Buddhas,
as well as Bodhisattvas and various devas,
and arranged them according to the ritual dharma.
Within the spokes of the wheel, one should inscribe the Sanskrit syllables of the mantra, but must not write the name.
If it is for a king, one must construct a large earthen mandala,
either sixteen or twenty-four cubits in size.
It reached as high as twenty-eight cubits;
because its dimensions differed from those of ordinary people,
there was fear that the King might give rise to suspicion.
He provisionally wrote down the names of all the devas on paper and affixed them beneath each of the honored ones,
so as to cause them to sever their doubts and give rise to right faith.
If one is able to write its name in Sanskrit script, it is most excellent and sublime; however,
if one does not know the Sanskrit characters,
it is also acceptable to inscribe it using the local script of the region.
From the center of the wheel,
draw upward a white eight-petaled lotus flower;
in the center of the flower, [use] gold or silver.
Paint a Golden Wheel Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa with the single-syllable dhāraṇī character *bhrūṃ* (悖嚕吽)— pronounced with a long vowel— and after this, paint first the Blazing Light Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
Great rays of light radiate from all the pores of his body.
Facing the Buddha directly across the mantra syllables,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Locanā, the Mother of the Buddhas, the color of a red lotus.
Each holds their respective insignia and mudrā.
Next, to the right of the Buddha, paint the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
of reddish-gold color, also holding his own insignia and mudrā.
To the left of the Buddha, paint the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi;
he is white-red in color and likewise holds his insignia.
All four deities sit in the half-lotus posture, facing one another.
Furthermore, to the right of Mañjuśrī, paint the Bodhisattva Acintyapāla-kumāra;
to the left of Mañjuśrī, paint the Bodhisattva Jñānarakṣa;
and to the right of Vajrapāṇi, paint the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī.
To the left of Vajrapāṇi, one should paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
each with their respective colors, emblems, mudrās, and facial expressions, as described for the eight great deities previously mentioned.
He recited in verse:
"The Uṣṇīṣa consists of a single syllable; It is the wondrous and supreme Lord, The blazing form and countenance of the Buddha, From whose pores rays of light fly forth and scatter."
The crown bears the marks of the five buddhas; the two hands are as those of Śākyamuni.
To the right is the Honored One Mañjuśrī, whose head is adorned with a topknot of the five wisdoms and who holds a blue lotus in his left hand, upon which stands a wisdom-vajra.
Holding a great sword of wisdom in her right hand,
she sits in the half-lotus posture before the Buddha Akṣobhya; her body is the color of a red lotus,
she holds the seal of the five eyes in her left hand, and her right hand forms the Tathāgata-fist.
To the left is Vajrapāṇi, his body white with a reddish tint;
his right hand holds an upturned lotus flower, upon which stand the five wisdoms, while his left hand holds the bell-seal. He sits in the half-lotus posture upon a lotus.
Next, the inconceivable [mudrā] is explained: The face is the color of vermilion-gold;
the two hands form inward-clasped fists.
The two index fingers (vāyu) are bent and brought together so that their fingernails touch back-to-back, and it is offered toward Mañjuśrī.
Furthermore, Trāṇaprajñā: her physical form is like a white lotus;
with the feathers of wisdom covering her heart, she extends her right hand straight upward toward the void.
She clearly manifests as Vidyujjvālākarālī, her complexion the color of jade.

The first two hands, representing concentration and wisdom, hold an unfurled lotus in the hand of concentration and display the gesture of fearlessness in the hand of wisdom; the latter two hands, representing concentration and wisdom,
hold a rosary in the hand of concentration and a water flask in the hand of wisdom.
Next, the visualization of Avalokiteśvara, also known as Cintāmaṇicakra:
In his left palm he holds a maṇi-jewel; his hands form the mudrās of Wisdom, Relaxation, Bestowal, and Vow.
His body is white with a reddish hue, and he abides within a great lotus flower.
Thus, outside these eight deities, place one [deity] in a circular boundary;
encircling the path of this boundary, write the mantras of four deities, namely:
Jvalanārci, Buddhalocanā, and the Bodhisattvī.
Behind Mañjuśrī and Vajrapāṇi, one should write the secret mantras using white powder mixed with gold and silver; these all penetrate the ultimate truth.
Outside the mantra, one should depict the nine planets and the great celestial lords.

That is to say: the Sun Deity, the Moon Deity, the five planets, the deities of eclipses, comets, as well as Mahābrahmā, the Śuddhāvāsakāyika gods, Nārāyaṇa, the General of the Gods, and Śakra Devendra, Lord of the Devas.
Behind the Buddha, one should paint Mahesvara Mahadeva together with eleven other deities,
totaling twelve honored ones,
arranged in a circle surrounding him.
Each has its own vehicle and each has its own object of grasping;
only those who have received the transmission of this Dharma know this.
Beyond these great heavens, one further establishes the path of the realms.
Outside the path, erect twelve single-pronged vajra-wands,
extending all the way to the outer rim,
to serve as the spokes of the golden wheel.
Within these spokes,
facing the Buddha before him,
one should proceed clockwise toward the right, following the path of the sun.
The positions of the signs are Cancer, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn;
these six signs are on the right side of the Buddha.
Furthermore, proceeding clockwise from behind the Buddha, they turn back toward the front of the Buddha.

Next is the House of the Treasure Vase (Kumbha), then the House of the Fish (Mīna), then the House of the Ram (Meṣa), then the House of the Bull (Vṛṣabha), then the House of the Twins (Mithuna), and then the House of the Crab (Karkaṭaka).
These six houses are situated to the left of the Buddha and connect with the House of the Lion (Siṃha); behind the Buddha, one should place the lunar mansion of Śravaṇā.
One should place the seven lunar mansions (nakṣatras) before the Buddha.
Outside these twelve palaces (dvādaśa-rāśi), one should arrange the twenty-eight lunar mansions,
each placed according to the sequence of its respective palace.
If one is performing the rite for a king to eliminate calamities, one should depict the full body of a deity.
For others, from commoners downward, when eliminating calamities, one should not depict the body of a deity;
rather, it is sufficient to establish their position by writing the deity's name in Sanskrit characters and marking it with the shape of a star.
Outside the twenty-eight lunar mansions, draw a circular rim surrounding them like the felloe of a wheel.
It should be golden in color, with a width and size proportionate to the shape of the wheel.
Upon this rim, depict the Eight Celestial Kings of the Directions.
Yāma-deva should be placed in front of the Buddha;
Vaiśravaṇa-deva should be placed behind the Buddha;
and Varuṇa-deva should be placed upon the rim behind Mañjuśrī.
Behind Vajrapāṇi, one should place the Gandharva King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
In the four corners are the four deva kings:
in the northeast corner is the Lord of the Desire Realm (Kāmeśvara).
In the southeast corner is the Fire Deity;
in the southwest corner is the Lord of Rākṣasas;
in the northwest corner is the Wind Deity.
Upon this empty space within the rim,
there are the Mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa in gold and silver script, as well as the four-line verse on dependent origination and the text of the Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
"Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations, and so on, up to: conditioned by birth are aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.
Furthermore, he wrote down the twelve phrases of cessation:
"With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; and so on, up to: with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease."
One should cause them to be distributed all across the rim.
Furthermore, one should draw one hundred and eight blue lotuses outside the wheel,
with the tips of their petals following the curvature of this wheel.
On each individual leaf, one should write the letter *A* (𑀅) in the Brāhmī script using gold, silver, or white powder;
gold and silver are most excellent.
Outside the four sides of the leaves and outside the boundary,
draw a surrounding boundary-path on all four edges;
upon this boundary-path, draw single-pronged vajras.
Joining them together in a continuous circle to enclose the perimeter constitutes the boundary.
Within this square boundary, at the four corners outside the wheel, there are empty spaces.
Paint the four Great Vidyārājas as external protectors.
Within the inner corner on the right side of the Buddha,
paint the four-armed Trailokyavijaya Vidyārāja, blue in color.
In the inner corner to the left of the Buddha,
one should paint the blue Acala Vidyārāja;
in the inner corner to the right of the Buddha’s back.
Paint the four-armed Aparājita Vidyārāja, purple-black in color,
in the inner left corner behind the Buddha.
Paint the four-armed Mahābala Ucchuṣma Vajra Vidyārāja, red in color.
These four Great Vidyārājas all sit upon precious circular rocks, surrounded by flames;
they are to be arranged according to the instructions in this manner.
It is titled "The Dharma Wheel of Secret Commands for Dispelling Calamities of All Tathāgatas.
Whenever there is distress,
it shall extend from the king above, down to the crown prince, the queen, and the court ladies.
Down to the hundred officials, monastics and laypeople, and the common masses—
should their natal stars be suppressed by the five planets, which move retrograde and remain stationary,
or should there be solar or lunar eclipses occurring above them;
When a comet, a planetary aberration, or a malevolent star invades a lunar mansion,
one should employ this very method therein:
adorn a clean room in a deep and secluded place.
Construct the maṇḍala;
do not allow many people to see or know of it.
If many people see or know of it, then one's prayers will be difficult to fulfill and calamities will not be averted.
If a king seeks to pacify calamities,
he should adorn a secluded hall and construct a maṇḍala.
Following the instructions, he should purify and decorate it according to the Dharma, as described in the sūtra.
Do not allow women, eunuchs, slaves, or base individuals to see it, for they would defile the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
This includes all such as animals, which are vessels of inauspiciousness.
If pigs, dogs, cats, or mice are present, do not allow them to see the pure *maṇḍala*.
If possible, enter the *maṇḍala* one by one in person and pray with utmost sincerity to the celestial deities being worshipped therein.
Recite the mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Tejorāśi without interruption day and night,
while also reciting the mantras of various deities;
at the very least, for three days and three nights.
For many days, or seven days and nights, or twice seven days and nights,
one should maintain the recitation with a sincere heart while simultaneously performing homa.
This is most excellent until a response is received in the form of auspicious signs or warnings.
One should know that calamities and obstacles will certainly be eliminated.
If one obtains the desired efficacy,
this is the mandala.
One must collect and discard them; they should not be kept for long.
Such is the rule of the original method.
If it is an earthen altar, one must scrape it away and sweep it clean.
They are sent into the long-flowing pure waters.
If one is unable to enter the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) oneself—
whether due to public or private official duties, or because of service to a sovereign— then [the rite may be performed on their behalf].
One may be serving those of noble rank or confined within the seclusion of the inner chambers;
or perhaps one’s physical strength is insufficient, or there are elders or children at home who are ill;
or one may have lowered oneself in status and lacks autonomy, or be residing elsewhere as a dependent with no home or place of one's own.
Alternatively, if it is difficult to establish [the practice] in a place frequented by those with wrong views,
evil people, or enemies, one should immediately seek out a person— whether a monastic or a layperson—
who clearly understands these teachings and instructions, and earnestly request them [to assist].
Provide whatever they require and have them perform the recitation on one's behalf.
With careful secrecy and sincere devotion, establish the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*).
Thereafter, reward their labor so that they may be filled with joy.
If circumstances are so pressing that one cannot construct an altar,
one should simply take a clean bed and spread it in a secluded, deep room, a pure location,
or within a monastery, and there install the wheel altar.
To the north, suspend an image of the Buddha-Cūḍāmaṇi-Śikhin Mañjuśrī, the Wheel-Turning King;
alternatively, it is also acceptable to face a single image of a wrathful king.
Adorn and arrange this maṇḍala with banners, streamers, and flower canopies.
Before the honored image, in the manner of a maṇḍala,
arrange offerings on all four sides according to the ritual: food and drink, fruits, milk porridge,
curd-rice, granulated sugar, ghee lamps, honey syrup, and sugarcane.
Various juices, such as those made from grapes, were arranged and displayed;
incense was burned and flowers scattered as offerings while the practitioner chanted with a sincere mind.
The person performing the rite wore pure white garments.
If the number of days is as previously stated, the calamity will surely be extinguished.
All ritual vessels for the offerings should be made of pure silver;
do not use white bronze or white porcelain, and do not use vessels that have been touched by defilement.
O Auspicious One, you must constantly recite the *Candraguhyatilaka-buddhoṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī* day and night without interruption.
For the incense to be burned, one should use aloeswood, white sandalwood, bdellium, frankincense, and white mugwort, blended together.
They were not limited to thousands or tens of thousands,
but reached as many as lakṣas or even three lakṣas of koṭis;
the count was limited only by the fulfillment of their vows.
Furthermore, there is no fixed number for the duration of the period;
one should also recite the mantra of Buddhalocanā and the mantras of the eight bodhisattvas, including Mañjuśrī and Vajrapāṇi.
At the beginning of each session, upon entering the maṇḍala hall...
First, each person shall recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times to invite [the deities] into the maṇḍala. Then,
one shall recite the mantras for the various devas and the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) seven times each.
While reciting with right mindfulness,
one should deeply arouse a mind of loving-kindness and constantly gaze upon the forms of the various deities on this wheel with the Buddha-eye.
With a humble heart, offer prayers, burn incense, and make vows to seek and receive grace and blessings.
One should not harbor a mind of subjugating wrath;
to do so would contradict the holy conclusion and be entirely inappropriate.
These are all celestial beings of great merit who practice the bodhisattva path.
"By the power of his vows, he has assumed this celestial body in order to benefit sentient beings, causing those stubborn and unruly beings to fear and thereby perform wholesome deeds.
How could one possibly take this inferior, lowly, minute portion of a layman's body— a body defiled like a grain of mustard seed?"
Yet to wish to subdue the celestial immortals who govern creation is impossible;
one must reflect carefully before acting, and treat them with reverence and awe.
Deeply giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings and those who are in extreme distress,
one should vow to liberate them and single-mindedly recite the Mantra of the Uṣṇīṣa of the Buddha of Blazing Radiance.
Only those with great merit shall be supreme.
I now proclaim this dhāraṇī, which says:
*saptakṣaṇi*. (At the end of "sapt," one should say "kṣaṇi. *kā* *mā*.
Śrīye namo ’hamantrabuddhānām | apratihatāśeṣasattvānām | Oṃ khaḥ || 1 ||
KHAKHA KHĪ KHĪ HŪṂ HŪṂ JVALA JVALA PRABHAVA PRABHAVA VAṂ.
Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha seḍhi svāta svāta svāhā. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā.
Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo viyurāhatebhyaḥ | Viyatsamayasambhavebhyaḥ | Oṃ ruru saparu jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvaduṣṭān saṃharaya svāhā. This is the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
The union of concentration and wisdom forms the hollow heart;
Open the wind and pinch the fire, with the two voids aligned and upright.
This is like the five eyes marking the seven recollections of that mantra; Seal the eyes and both sides.
Between the eyebrows is the Buddha-eye, the compassionate eye of the Buddha.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, by means of the blue lotus mudrā, one performs the seven recollections and the three invocations;
having summoned them, they are carried across by the wind of wisdom.
Visualize yourself as the Lion King, descending upon the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to fulfill all aspirations.
Recite his mantra: Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Hī hī kumārakamāraga | Vimuktipatrasvādhyāya | Samāra samāra | Pratijñāna svāhā || The Heart Mantra is: [Omitted]
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi: the mudrā is as explained below;
the two water fingers cross within, the earth and fire fingers are joined and held upright, the two space fingers are likewise like the earth, and the wind fingers form the shape of five prongs.
This is the mark of the great secret.
The mantra of Vajrapāṇi is: *Namaḥ samantavajra-jvālana-mahā-rūṣaṇa hūṃ*. This is the heart-mantra.
Furthermore, for the Wisdom of Rescue and Protection:
With the hand of Samādhi in the vajra-fist posture, sit upright with it resting at the side of the waist;
extend the five fingers of the Wisdom hand straight upward to cover the heart, and raise the space-wheel (thumb) vertically into the air.
Furthermore, for the Seal of Inconceivable Wisdom (*acintya-prajñā-mudrā*), as described below:
Interlace the fingers of the hands of concentration and wisdom within; join them together to form a fist-seal.
Extend the two index fingers (*vāyu*) separately and bend them so that their third joints face one another.
Cause the thumbs to face away from each other; the two index fingers are held side by side and upright.
Furthermore, as for the practitioner who follows the instructions, the mudrā has already been explained previously;
the seal of the Bodhisattva Prajñājñānarakṣa is also clarified as before.
Next is the Honored One Bhr̥kuṭī; her mudrā is as described below:
join the fists of concentration and wisdom internally, raise the vāyu fingers to cross over the tips of the other joints;
this can eliminate all calamities and disasters, and utterly extinguish all evils and sufferings.
Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara is also known as the Wish-Fulfilling Wheel;
his concentration and wisdom are bound in a vajra-knot.
His two fingers of patience and aspiration are like lotus petals, while the two winds are pressed together like jewels; the wheel of space is joined like a banner.
Raising the earth and crossing over the upper joint—this is called the Seal of the Small Mind (*sūkṣmacitta-mudrā*).
Then recite the mantra: Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ padma-maṇi-jvālā hūṃ || This is the Heart of Hearts (*hṛdaya-hṛdaya*).
Oṃ vāranaprabhaṃ hūṃ. This is the mantra of Maheśvara Deva-rāja; here it is called Mahesvara (the Great Sovereign).

*Namo maṃtra-bhūtānām oṃ ī ī hi ma hi śvara ya svāhā*. Furthermore, the mantra of Īśāna, the Lord of the Desire Realm, is called "The Lesser Īśāna": *Namo maṃtra-bhūtānām oṃ ī ī hi ma hi śvara ya svāhā*. Again, the mantra of Īśāna, the Sovereign of the Desire Realm, is called "The Lesser Īśāna."
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ rudrāya svāhā. This is the mantra of the Great Brahmā Deva-rāja.
*Namo maṃtra-bhāṣita-buddhānām | Oṃ mahā-maheśvari īkṣe he svāhā.* This is the mantra for summoning the deities of the twelve zodiac signs (*dvādaśa-rāśi*).
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ gṛhe śvāriye prapratājuśrīmāye ṭiṭṭe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā || This is the mantra for summoning the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*).

Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ āḥ stha-viśeṣa-nidhāna-nīrṇaye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra for summoning all the devas, the seven planets, the twelve zodiac signs, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the various grahas, and the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī).
Furthermore, to clarify the seals of the various devas:

The seal of Maheśvara has the wisdom fingers extended as five wheels; resting his cheek, he remains solemnly in samādhi with the five wheels extended, holding the space-finger upon the wind-finger joint.
This is the mudrā of Mahābrahmā: Forming the upright seal while reciting the root mantra, fix the hands into a single fist;
extend the fire finger and bend the wind finger at the joint, like the appearance of a standing spear. This is the mudrā of Īśāna.
The concentration and wisdom are firmly joined; the two wheels of emptiness are erected together like a banner.
Without changing the previous seal-form, all seals of the planets and stars have the void and fire intersecting one another.
Placing the fingers upon the back of the hand—this is the universal ancestral seal (*sarva-pūrva-mudrā*).
Furthermore, regarding the deities of the external world, the secret mudrās of Īśāna have already been explained;
next, the seals of the remaining deities shall be described.
The Eastern Lord Dhṛtarāṣṭra raises his right hand into a fist and covers it with the left, crossing them at the waist;
this is called the Mudrā of Water Protection.
With the hands joined in fists internally, the water-wheels (the little fingers) are extended and held upright together.
For the visualization of movement, music, and light, this is the mudrā of the Gandharvas:
with the palms facing upward at the heart, the fire and space fingers are joined together in the shape of a triangle; this mudrā is named Agni.
The Wisdom Hand (right hand) has its four fingers extended like wheels; the space-finger (thumb) is placed horizontally across the palm.
The wind-finger (ring finger) is bent to summon with three beckoning gestures.
This is the mudrā for summoning the Fire God at the southern gate, the Lord of the Flaming Demons (Yama); its seal is as clarified below.
Joining the two hands to form a lotus, with the earth and wind [elements] hanging down into the palms like the *daṇḍa* (staff) gesture,
this is called the insignia of the Lord of Death (*Mṛtyurāja*).
Furthermore, it is taught as the seal of the Rākṣasa King in the southwest direction.
The palms of Samādhi and Prajñā joined like lotuses, with the two waters entering and intersecting within the moon;
next, in the western direction of the Nāgas, the fists of Samādhi and Prajñā are joined inwardly,
while the two winds are like interlocking rings— this is the seal of all the water-nāgas.
Forming a fist with the hands firmly clenched, visualize the earth and water as being erected like banners;
imagine those banners fluttering and moving.
Next, for the protection of the directions, starting from the north—the most excellent direction—is the mudrā of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
With the hands of samādhi and wisdom, interlace the fingers within to form fists;
join the two "fires" (the index fingers) at their tips and contract them into the shape of a jewel.
These are the mudrās of the various devas; bind them with mindfulness to summon them.
Instruct the guardians of the maṇḍala so that those in distress may all have their wishes fulfilled.
Having completed the invocation of Mahādeva,
next recite the verses of dependent origination clearly three or seven times.
"All phenomena arise from conditions; The Tathāgata has declared their cause, And their cessation as well—this is the Great Śramaṇa’s teaching.
Thus he spoke this verse on the twelvefold dependent origination, And he also recollected it in its proper sequence.
In the arena of writing, one should recite and remember each and every link without forgetting:
ignorance conditions formations; formations condition consciousness;
consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises.
Birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Furthermore, the phrase "cessation" refers to the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination:
with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
With the cessation of grasping, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases.
With the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease.
[This is inscribed] upon one hundred and eight lotus petals outside the wheel.
One should cause each of the Brahmī syllables, beginning with the letter A (𑀅), to pervade [the body].
At every time of recitation,
one should make a vow and address the assembly of holy ones.
Holding an incense burner in one's hands, approach with utmost sincerity and remain kneeling for a long time.
Before the Buddha, recite this text of vows as follows.
The master of the ritual site must personally enter the sanctuary at the three periods of each day to offer these prayers.
The practitioner must also personally recite it until it is mastered.
One must always utter this vow, addressing the disciple by name— using their secular name for a layperson,
or "Bhikṣu [Name]" if they are a monk.
If [addressing] a high minister or official, say: "The name and title of such-and-such official.
If [addressing] a king, say: "The name of the ruler of such-and-such kingdom. I now take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and the assembly of noble beings of the ocean-like gathering.
I reverently address the Tathāgata Universal Radiance of the Pure Dharma-body,
universally proclaiming this to all Buddhas and the assembly of great Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time,
as well as to all worthy and holy ones, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
The five classes of ṛṣis possessing supernatural powers, the nine grahas, the great devas,
the lords of the twelve zodiac signs, the twenty-eight lunar mansions,
the various sages and numina, and the four great vidyārājas.
The Eight World-Protecting Devas along with their retinues;
the local deities, mountain spirits, and virtuous guardians of the Dharma;
the officials of the karmic paths and the presiding stars of one's natal destiny.
Now that I have encountered these calamities and transformations, I shall state each of my requested vows in detail:
such-and-such matters are being oppressed [by obstacles].
O Great Deity who Roams through Space, I pray that you will comply with the Buddha’s instructions.
Having accepted my invitation, may you all come to this assembly;
moved by my single-minded sincerity,
may you give rise to hearts of joy and eliminate such urgent calamities and misfortunes for me, [Name].
Having received the compassionate power of protection and guidance from the Great Sage, I have encountered this teaching,
which delivers us and all sentient beings from the karmic suffering of saṃsāra.
I pray only that the deities of the nine planets [will likewise grant their aid].
Relying on the Buddha’s wheel, may calamities be transformed into blessings.
Grant me fearlessness so that I may dwell in peace and happiness;
may we together form a retinue for Bodhi in the future.
May we forever abandon love and hatred and mutually benefit one another.

Having prayed, "May you grant me fearlessness so that I may be auspicious," one must constantly and diligently recite this prayer three times each day, never ceasing; whether at three sessions, four sessions, or for extended periods daily.
Make vows and offer supplications to eliminate lack of sincerity;
if one is negligent or indolent, what is sought will not be granted.
Those who encounter calamity must make vows with diligent sincerity.
On the final day of the site-consecration (*maṇḍala*), in accordance with the teachings of the mantra-dharma,
perform *homa* oblations using ghee, honey, curd, milk,
and wood; furthermore, offer food to the deities of the eight directions as well as to all spirits and ghosts.
Furthermore, within a single basin of water,
place various kinds of sweet foods, fruits, sweets, and crisp delicacies;
all must be broken into pieces while reciting the *Yamāntaka* mantra and generating a mind of compassion.
Recite the empowerment mantra twenty-one times, or forty-nine times, or one hundred and eight times.
Then, take [the offering] outside the city walls or outside the residence and pour it onto clean ground to be given as food to nameless and rankless spirits and deities.
Alternatively, one may divide it and cast it into rivers, streams, or flowing waters.
For those who act in accordance with these instructions,
no calamity or misfortune shall fail to be extinguished and eradicated.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Since I first heard this teaching,
I have constantly expounded it in this manner for the sake of sentient beings."
May all Tathāgatas bear witness to me.
Having completed the proclamation of the Wheel of Dharma for the Elimination of Calamities through these injunctions,
you hosts of devas should respectfully and obediently practice according to the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, having heard this sutra being preached, all the devas were filled with great joy;
with one voice and in unison, they all spoke these words:
"We respectfully rely upon your holy instructions and dare not transgress them."
Having received it with faith and practiced it accordingly, they paid homage and departed.
